6.2 Collection method is not origin.

Evaluating OSINT: Why It Matters and How to Do It Right - SOS Intelligence
Evaluating OSINT: Why It Matters and How to Do It Right
In short, evaluation is what separates noise from insight. It’s not just a good practice – it’s a critical step that determines the overall value and credibility of your intelligence output.

One widely recognised method for evaluating sources and information is the Admiralty Code, also known as the NATO Source Reliability and Information Credibility grading system. It uses a two-part alphanumeric rating to assess:

Once you’ve identified what you’re looking for and established your evaluation criteria, the next step is to put those principles into practice. Evaluating sources effectively requires both critical thinking and a methodical approach. Below are some techniques that can help analysts assess the credibility, authenticity, and relevance of open source material.

Even with a solid framework and a set of reliable techniques, OSINT evaluation often comes down to the fine details – the subtle clues, the consistency checks, and the instinct honed by experience. This section offers practical, hands-on advice to help you refine your evaluation skills and avoid common pitfalls.

Maintain a record of how you’ve assessed each source – including decisions around credibility, context, and any verification steps taken. This is especially important in collaborative environments or when intelligence may need to be defended later. Tools like analyst notebooks, spreadsheets, or structured databases can help you track this clearly.
Structured templates and tools from the OSINT community that support methodical evaluation and reporting.
Absence of a Structured Framework

Whether you’re using the Admiralty Code, applying structured frameworks, or leveraging specialised tools, the goal remains the same: to produce intelligence that is accurate, reliable, and actionable. Evaluation isn’t a final step in the OSINT process – it’s woven throughout.

Is the content neutral, or does it show bias? Be wary of emotionally charged language, persuasive tone, or content designed to provoke. Identifying whether the source has an agenda can help you judge how much weight to give the information.

Analysing tone, language, and publication history can reveal bias or intent that may affect credibility.

In the Protocol's terms, gaining possession of online information through a screenshot, a conversion to PDF, a download or another form of capture.
Filings to, and records kept by, a regulator, statutory registry or court, retrieved from that body's own system
Anything beyond the third party's own access; the content of a filing it describes, until the filing itself is retrieved
4.2 What common US filings do and do not show.

Establish that the item is what it appears to be. A filing retrieved from the registry's own system is a different item from a copy of it hosted elsewhere. Check metadata, and compare dates inside the document with the page's dates.

A news report of a filing is evidence of what the reporter wrote. Its origin is OSINT_SOURCED. When the filing itself is retrieved from the regulator's own system, it becomes a second evidence item with origin REGULATORY_PUBLIC_RECORD. An evidence item names only what the researcher actually read.
A filing to, or a record kept by, a regulator, statutory registry or court, retrieved from that body's own system
An official publication of a public body or public-sector institution, issued in its official capacity and not as a filing to a regulator
A filing is still the filer's own account. REGULATORY_PUBLIC_RECORD says where it was filed, not that it is true.
A subject's filing and the same subject's press release are one originating source for facts only the subject can supply. Together they do not make a claim CORROBORATED (see

Filings are the filers' own accounts. A body's acceptance of a filing does not by itself establish that its content is true; for Form ADV the SEC states that accepting the form is not a finding that it was completed correctly.

Every evidence item records its capture date and time, the artefact's own publication or filing date, and the as-of date of the value, using the date vocabulary of the Evidence & Provenance Standard. These dates are never substituted for one another.
A copy of a filing hosted by an aggregator.
It is OSINT_SOURCED until the filing is retrieved from the regulator's or registry's own system.

IntelTechniques Workbook / Casefile
Case Study: Misidentification in the Boston Marathon Bombing

The 2013 Boston Marathon bombing provides a powerful example of how poor OSINT evaluation can lead to serious consequences. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, online communities – particularly Reddit – attempted to crowdsource intelligence to help identify the perpetrators.
This case shows that while open source intelligence can be powerful, it must be used responsibly. Without evaluation, it’s just noise – and in high-stakes situations, that noise can do real damage.

突き合わせ・推定.quote: DERIVED and ESTIMATED values have no origin of their own. Their origin is the set of origins of their inputs.
For DERIVED and ESTIMATED values, validation covers the inputs and the correct application of the rule or method. Validation never turns an ESTIMATED value into an OBSERVED one.

Reliability and credibility grades are judgments. Irwin and Mandel (2019) argue that the Admiralty-style scales mask subjectivity and recommend numeric probability estimates and periodic re-evaluation. This standard keeps ordinal grades for sources and information, requires reasons for each, and uses numeric ranges for likelihood judgments.
